entries.3f071f54aed2ea112b9f8e3a26b1934c149dc852: <div sID="gen12959" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="123" osisID="Ps.123" sID="Ps.123"/> <div eID="gen12959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12960" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12961" type="x-p"/> This psalm was penned at a time when the church of God was brought low and trampled upon; some think it was when the Jews were captives in Babylon, though that was not the only time that they were insulted over by the proud. The psalmist begins as if he spoke for himself only (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.1">ver. 1</reference>), but presently speaks in the name of the church. Here is, I. Their expectation of mercy from God, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Their plea for mercy with God,, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.3-Ps.123.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. In singing it we must have our eye up to God's favour with a holy concern, and then an eye down to men's reproach with a holy contempt.
entries.44b532a5622ae59b6aa363239d9dcc785b794cf5: <div eID="gen12961" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12960" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments.</title> <div sID="gen12962" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O thou that dwellest in the heavens. <hi type="super">2</hi> Behold, as the eyes of servants <hi type="italic">look</hi> unto the hand of their masters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress; so our eyes <hi type="italic">wait</hi> upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, until that he have mercy upon us. <hi type="super">3</hi> Have mercy upon us, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , have mercy upon us: for we are exceedingly filled with contempt. <hi type="super">4</hi> Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorning of those that are at ease, <hi type="italic">and</hi> with the contempt of the proud. <div eID="gen12962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12963" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen12963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12964" type="x-p"/> I. The solemn profession which God's people make of faith and hope in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Observe, 1. The title here given to God: <hi type="italic">O thou that dwellest in the heavens.</hi> Our Lord Jesus has taught us, in prayer, to have an eye to God as <hi type="italic">our Father in heaven;</hi> not that he is confined there, but there especially he manifests his glory, as the King in his court. Heaven is a place of prospect and a place of power; he that dwells there beholds thence all the calamities of his people and thence can send to save them. Sometimes God seems to have forsaken the earth, and the enemies of God's people ask, <hi type="italic">Where is now your God?</hi> But then they can say with comfort, <hi type="italic">Our God is in the heavens. O thou that sittest in the heavens</hi> (so some), sittest as Judge there; for <hi type="italic">the Lord has prepared his throne in the heavens,</hi> and to that throne injured innocency may appeal. 2. The regard here had to God. The psalmist himself <hi type="italic">lifted up his eyes</hi> to him. The eyes of a good man are <hi type="italic">ever towards the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Ps. xxv. 15</reference>. In every prayer we lift up our soul, the eye of our soul, to God, especially in trouble, which was the case here. The <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> of the people <hi type="italic">waited on the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.123.2">v. 2</reference>. We find mercy coming towards a people <hi type="italic">when the eyes of man, as of all the tribes of Israel, are towards the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.9.1">Zech. ix. 1</reference>. The eyes of the body are heaven-ward. <hi type="italic">Os homini sublime dedit—To man he gave an erect mien,</hi> to teach us which way to direct the eyes of the mind. <hi type="italic">Our eyes wait on the Lord,</hi> the eye of desire and prayer, the begging eye, and the eye of dependence, hope, and expectation, the longing eye. Our eyes must wait upon God as <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">our God, until that he have mercy upon us.</hi> We desire mercy from him, we hope he will show us mercy, and we will continue our attendance on him till the mercy come. This is illustrated (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.2">v. 2</reference>) by a similitude: Our eyes are to God <hi type="italic">as the eyes of a servant,</hi> and <hi type="italic">handmaid, to the hand of their master and mistress.</hi> The eyes of a servant are, (1.) To his master's directing hand, expecting that he will appoint him his work, and cut it out for him, and show him how he must do it. <hi type="italic">Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?</hi> (2.) To his supplying hand. Servants look to their master, or their mistress, for their portion of meat in due season, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.15">Prov. xxxi. 15</reference>. And to God must we look for daily bread, for grace sufficient; from him we must receive it thankfully. (3.) To his assisting hand. If the servant cannot do his work himself, where must he look for help but to his master? And in the strength of the Lord God we must go forth and go on. (4.) To his protecting hand. If the servant meet with opposition in his work, if he be questioned for what he does, if he be wronged and injured, who should bear him out and right him, but his master that set him on work? The people of God, when they are persecuted, may appeal to their Master, <hi type="italic">We are thine; save us.</hi> (5.) To his correcting hand. If the servant has provoked his master to beat him, he does not call for help against his master, but looks at the hand that strikes him, till it shall say, "It is enough; I will not contend for ever." The people of God were now under his rebukes; and whither should they turn but to him that <hi type="italic">smote them?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa. ix. 13</reference>. To whom should they make supplication but to their Judge? They will not do as Hagar did, who ran away from her mistress when she put some hardships upon her (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.6">Gen. xvi. 6</reference>), but they submit themselves to and humble themselves under God's mighty hand. (6.) To his rewarding hand. The servant expects his wages, his <hi type="italic">well-done,</hi> from his master. Hypocrites have their eye to the world's hand; thence <hi type="italic">they have their reward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.2">Matt. vi. 2</reference>); but true Christians have their eye to God as their rewarder. <div eID="gen12964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12965" type="x-p"/> II. The humble address which God's people present to him in their calamitous condition (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.3-Ps.123.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), wherein, 1. They sue for mercy, not prescribing to God what he shall do for them, nor pleading any merit of their own why he should do it for them, but, <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon us, O Lord! have mercy upon us.</hi> We find little mercy with men; their <hi type="italic">tender mercies are cruel;</hi> there are <hi type="italic">cruel mockings.</hi> But this is our comfort, that <hi type="italic">with the Lord there is mercy</hi> and we need desire no more to relieve us, and make us easy, than the mercy of God. Whatever the troubles of the church are, God's mercy is a sovereign remedy. 2. They set forth their grievances: <hi type="italic">We are exceedingly filled with contempt.</hi> Reproach is the wound, the burden, they complain of. Observe, (1.) Who were reproached: "We, who have our eyes up to thee." Those who are owned of God are often despised and trampled on by the world. Some translate the words which we render, <hi type="italic">those that are at ease,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the proud,</hi> so as to signify the persons that are scorned and contemned. "Our soul is troubled to see how those that are at peace, and the excellent ones, are scorned and despised." The saints are a peaceable people and yet are abused (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Ps. xxxv. 20</reference>), the excellent ones of the earth and yet undervalued, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.1-Lam.4.2">Lam. iv. 1, 2</reference>. (2.) Who did reproach them. Taking the words as we read them, they were the epicures who lived at ease, carnal sensual people, <reference osisRef="Job.12.5">Job xii. 5</reference>. The scoffers are such as walk after their own lusts and serve their own bellies, and the proud such as set God himself at defiance and had a high opinion of themselves; they trampled on God's people, thinking they magnified themselves by vilifying them. (3.) To what degree they were reproached: "<hi type="italic">We are filled,</hi> we are surfeited with it. <hi type="italic">Our soul is exceedingly filled with it.</hi>" The enemies thought they could never jeer them enough, nor say enough to make them despicable; and they could not but lay it to heart; it was a sword in their bones, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Ps. xlii. 10</reference>. Note, [1.] Scorning and contempt have been, and are, and are likely to be, the lot of God's people in this world. Ishmael mocked Isaac, which is called <hi type="italic">persecuting</hi> him; and so it is now, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Gal. iv. 29</reference>. [2.] In reference to the scorn and contempt of men it is matter of comfort that there is mercy with God, mercy to our good names when they are barbarously used. <hi type="italic">Hear, O our God! for we are despised.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.123"/> <div eID="gen12965" type="x-p"/>

entries.e1b88209d30819de51f74d3db4863352a48da52f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6999"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 123</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.4">Psa 123:1-4</reference>. An earnest and expecting prayer for divine aid in distress.</title> <div sID="gen10741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6999"/>1. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou that dwellest--</hi>literally, "sittest as enthroned" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.2.4">Psa 2:4</reference>; 113:4, 5). <div eID="gen10742" type="x-p"/>
entries.4da720b9616b388d98a2903ed8c786a95f244ac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7000"/><div sID="gen10743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7000"/>2. Deference, submission, and trust, are all expressed by the figure. In the East, servants in attending on their masters are almost wholly directed by signs, which require the closest observance of the hands of the latter. The servants of God should look (1) to His directing hand, to appoint them their work; (2) to His supplying hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.28">Psa 104:28</reference>), to give them their portion in due season; (3) to His protecting hand, to right them when wronged; (4) to His correcting hand (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.6">1Pe 5:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.16.6">Ge 16:6</reference>); (<reference osisRef="Gen.16.5">5</reference>) to His rewarding hand. <div eID="gen10743" type="x-p"/>
entries.87401ea7c6b6153ca604f5bfe9c9aa285f13cd07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7001"/><div sID="gen10744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7001"/><hi type="bold">3. contempt--</hi>was that of the heathen, and, perhaps, Samaritans (<reference osisRef="Neh.1.3">Ne 1:3</reference>; 2:19). <div eID="gen10744" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e80613fd0c5ac441a08493c37e42967af132711: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7002"/><div sID="gen10745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7002"/><hi type="bold">4. of those that are at ease--</hi>self-complacently, disregarding God's law, and despising His people. <chapter eID="Ps.123"/>

entries.66d92095fb89d6f37e5103bd969a54db6862d542: <div eID="gen23043" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23044" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23045" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23045" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23044" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23046" type="x-p"/> The prayer and faith of the godly, <reference osisRef="Psa.123.1">Psa 123:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.123.2">Psa 123:2</reference>. They desire to be delivered from contempt, <reference osisRef="Psa.123.3">Psa 123:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.123.4">Psa 123:4</reference>. <div eID="gen23046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23047" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is probably a complaint of the captives in Babylon relative to the contempt and cruel usage they received. The author is uncertain. <div eID="gen23047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23049" type="x-p"/> Unto thee lift I up mine eyes - We have no hope but in thee; our eyes look upward; we have expectation from thy mercy alone.
entries.5a9cb2a095d50272ffa0e8b065746ff734b485b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23050" type="x-p"/> As the eyes of servants - We now wait for thy commands, feeling the utmost readiness to obey them when made known to us. The words may be understood as the language of dependence also. As slaves expect their support from their masters and mistresses, so do we ours from thee, O Lord! Or, As servants look to their masters and mistresses, to see how they do their work, that they may do it in the same way; so do we, O Lord, that we may learn of thee, and do thy work in thy own Spirit, and after thy own method. Some think that there is a reference here to the chastisement of slaves by their masters, who, during the time they are receiving it, keep their eyes fixed on the hand that is inflicting punishment upon them, professing deep sorrow, and entreating for mercy. And this sense seems to be countenanced by the following words: -
entries.7865cf3a71e54adf939955e001b0ff9f5d966853: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23051" type="x-p"/> Have mercy upon us, O Lord - Chastise us no more; we will no more revolt against thee. <div eID="gen23051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23052" type="x-p"/> We are exceedingly filled with contempt - We not only suffer grievously from our captivity, but are treated in the most contemptuous maner by our masters.
entries.9998bd55ea197929b98006beb1e2cdf8403c557c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23053" type="x-p"/> Those that are at ease - The Babylonians, who, having subdued all the people of the neighboring nations, lived at ease, had none to contend with them, and now became luxurious, indolent, and insolent: they were contemptuous and proud.  <chapter eID="Ps.123"/> <div eID="gen23053" type="x-p"/>

entries.0825a13232d48e4eb1d6f581fda1f09b8de8a61e: <div eID="gen10180" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Upward Glance to the Lord in Times of Contempt</title> <div sID="gen10181" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is joined to the preceding Psalm by the community of the divine name <hi type="italic">Jahve our God</hi>. Alsted (died 1638) gives it the brief, ingenious inscription <hi type="italic">oculus sperans</hi>. It is an upward glance of waiting faith to Jahve under tyrannical oppression. The fact that this Psalm appears in a rhyming form, “as scarcely any other piece in the Old Testament” (Reuss), comes only from those inflexional rhymes which creep in of themselves in the tephilla style.
entries.d3ffcf465814abb3a36ee5eda0ea8e2eb2e8987b: <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.2">Psa 123:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10182" type="x-p"/> The destinies of all men, and in particular of the church, are in the hand of the King who sits enthroned in the unapproachable glory of the heavens and rules over all things, and of the Judge who decides all things. Up to Him the poet raises his eyes, and to Him the church, together with which he may call Him “Jahve our God,” just as the eyes of servants are directed towards the hand of their lord, the eyes of a maid towards the hand of her mistress; for this hand regulates the whole house, and they wait upon their winks and signs with most eager attention. Those of Israel are Jahve’s servants, Israel the church is Jahve’s maid. In His hand lies its future. At length He will take compassion on His own. Therefore its longing gaze goes forth towards Him, without being wearied, until He shall graciously turn its distress. With reference to the <hi type="italic">i</hi> of היּשׁבי, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1">Psa 114:1</reference>-8. אדוניהם is their common lord; for since in the antitype the sovereign Lord is meant, it will be conceived of as <hi type="italic">plur. excellentiae</hi>, just as in general it occurs only rarely (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.2">Gen 19:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.18">Gen 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.4">Jer 27:4</reference>) as an actual plural.
entries.eb05e1bd16f81d802fa361ba6c771db0a3588c5b: <reference osisRef="Ps.123.3-Ps.123.4">Psa 123:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen10182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10183" type="x-p"/> The second strophe takes up the “be gracious unto us” as it were in echo. It begins with a <hi type="italic">Kyrie eleison</hi>, which is confirmed in a <hi type="italic">crescendo</hi> manner after the form of steps. The church is already abundantly satiated with ignominy. רב is an abstract “much,” and רבּה, <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Psa 62:3</reference>, something great (vid., Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Lehrbuch</hi>, §624). The subjectivizing, intensive להּ accords with <reference osisRef="Ps.120.6">Psa 120:6</reference> - probably an indication of one and the same author. בּוּז is strengthened by לעג, like בּז in Eze 36:4. The article of הלּעג is restrospectively demonstrative: full of such scorn of the haughty (Ew. §290, <hi type="italic">d</hi>). הבּוּז is also retrospectively demonstrative; but since a repetition of the article for the fourth time would have been inelegant, the poet here says לגאיונים with the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi>, which serves as a circumlocution of the genitive. The Masora reckons this word among the fifteen “words that are written as one and are to be read as two.” The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> runs viz., לגאי יונים, <hi type="italic">superbis oppressorum</hi> (יונים, <hi type="italic">part. Kal</hi>, like היּונה Zep 3:1, and frequently). But apart from the consideration that instead of גּאי, from the unknown גּאה, it might more readily be pointed גּאי, from גּאה (a form of nouns indicating defects, contracted גּא), this genitival construction appears to be far-fetched, and, inasmuch as it makes a distinction among the oppressors, inappropriate. The poet surely meant לגאיונים or לגּאיונים. This word גּאיון (after the form רעיון, אביון, עליון) is perhaps an intentional new formation of the poet. Saadia interprets it after the Talmudic לגיון, <hi type="italic">legio</hi>; but how could one expect to find such a Grecized Latin word (λεγεών) in the Psalter! dunash ben-Labrat (about 960) regards גאיונים as a compound word in the signification of הגּאים היונים. In fact the poet may have chosen the otherwise unused adjectival form גּאיונים because it reminds one of יונים, although it is not a compound word like דּביונים. If the Psalm is a Maccabaean Psalm, it is natural to find in לגאיונים an allusion to the despotic domination of the יונים.  <chapter eID="Ps.123"/> <div eID="gen10183" type="x-p"/>

entries.84af5714f2dda5f44aa43d4e0d452f0247c011ed:
PSALM 123
In this Psalm, the faithful oppressed with the cruel tyranny of their enemies, beseech God to deliver them, there being no other source of hope left for them except in his protection.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 123:1-4
1. I lift up my eyes to thee, who dwellest in the heavens. 2. Behold! as the eyes of servants look
“Look” is a supplement taken from the French version.
to the hand of their roadsters; as the eyes of a handmaid look to the hand of her mistress, so do our eyes to Jehovah our God, until he have mercy upon us. 3. Have mercy upon us O Jehovah have mercy upon us; for we are greatly cloyed with reproach. 4. Our soul is in itself greatly cloyed with the mockery of men who are rich, and with the contempt of the proud.
 
1. I lift my eyes to thee, who dwellest in the heavens. It is uncertain at what time, or even by what Prophet, this Psalm was composed. I do not think it probable that David was its author; because, when he bewails the persecutions which he suffered in the time of Saul, it is usual with him to inter-pose some particular references to himself. My opinion, then, rather is, that this form of prayer was composed for all the godly by some Prophet, either when the Jews were captives in Babylon, or when Antiochus Epiphanes exercised towards them the most relentless cruelty. Be this as it may, the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration the Prophet delivered it to the people, calls upon us to have recourse to God, when — ever wicked men unrighteously and proudly persecute, not one or two of the faithful only, but the whole body of the Church. Moreover, God is here expressly called the God who dwelleth in the heavens, not simply to teach his people to estimate the divine power as it deserves, but also that, when no hope of aid is left for them on earth, yea rather, when their condition is desperate, just as if they were laid in the grave, or as if they were lost in a labyrinth, they should then remember that the power of God remains in heaven in unimpaired and infinite perfection. Thus these words seem to contain a tacit contrast between the troubled and confused state of this world and God’s heavenly kingdom, from whence he so manages and governs all things, that whenever it pleases him, he calms all the agitations of the world, comes to the rescue of the desperate and the despairing, restores light by dispelling darkness, and raises up such as were cast down and laid prostrate on the ground. This the Prophet confirms by the verb lift up; which intimates, that although all worldly resources fail us, we must raise our eyes upward to heaven, where God remains unchangeably the same, despite the mad impetuosity of men in turning all things here below upside down.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains a description of the great agony and di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stress of Gods people, and of their carriage under it.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 UNto thee <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Unto thee onely, because all other persons either can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not, or will not, help me.</ns0:note> lift I up mine eyes, O thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 115. 3.</ns0:note> that dwellest in the heavens.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Behold, as the eyes of servants <ns0:hi>look</ns0:hi> unto the hand of their masters <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either, 1. for supply of their wants, which comes from their masters hand: or, 2. for pity, the hand being the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strument whereby masters commonly correct their servants, and looking to the hand may express the posture of one sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plicating for mercy: or rather, 3. for help and defence a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst their oppressors. For servants were unable to defend themselves, and were not allowed to wear defensive weapons, but expected and had protection from their masters in case of injury. For this phrase of <ns0:hi>having ones eyes towards another</ns0:hi> both in this and other sacred Books, constantly notes expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctation and desire of help from them, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 25. 15. & 69. 4. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 17. 7. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 23. 27. and oft elsewhere. And the phrase of Gods <ns0:hi>having mercy</ns0:hi> upon another, doth most com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly signifie that act or effect of his mercy in helping and delivering him.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> as the eyes of a maiden unto the hand of her mistress: so our eyes <ns0:hi>wait</ns0:hi> upon the LORD our God, until that he have mercy upon us <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Until he graciously help and save us.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy upon us: for we are exceedingly filled with contempt <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">With opprobrious words and injuries.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Our soul is exceedingly filled with the scorn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>The <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                           <ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lent.</ns0:hi> 2 Kings 9. 28.</ns0:note> those that are at ease, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> with the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt of the proud <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">With the scornful and contemptuous carriage of thine and our enemies, who live in great ease and glory, whilst we, thy people, are overwhelmed with manifold calamities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Poole.heading: PSAL. CXXIII. A song of degrees.
